questions.q: How many times brighter in X-rays is an X-class flare than a C-class flare?
questions.do: Read the note under the X-ray flashes, last 24 hours chart.
questions.a: 100 times. Each step up the scale (A, B, C, M, X) is ten times brighter, and X is two steps above C: 10 × 10 = 100.

questions.q: For the fastest storm cloud ever measured, how much does a light cloud differ from a big heavy cloud?
questions.do: In Launch a solar storm, drag Solar wind it ploughs through to 400 km/s. Click Fastest measured with Big heavy cloud selected and read Reaches Earth in and Arrives at. Then click Light cloud.
questions.a: Heavy cloud: about 19.3 h, arriving at about 1,352 km/s. Light cloud: about 28.2 h, arriving at about 818 km/s. The wind drags harder on a light cloud, so it slows down more.

questions.q: How do you work out the warning time that the spacecraft at L1 gives us? Use the May 2024 storm as an example.
questions.do: Read the text in The solar wind section, then find the May 2024 row in the How far to trust it table.
questions.a: Warning time = 1,500,000 km ÷ wind speed. In May 2024 the wind blew at 750–950 km/s, giving only about 26–33 minutes of warning. Faster wind means less warning.

questions.q: Why are storms more likely when the Bz tile shows a number below zero?
questions.do: Read the Magnetic field Bz tile and the text in The solar wind section.
questions.a: When Bz is below zero, the wind's magnetic field points south. It links with Earth's field and pours energy in: the page says the door is open. When it points north, the door is shut.

questions.q: In 1859 the Carrington storm cloud reached Earth in 17.6 hours. According to the model, how fast would a cloud need to be launched to do that in normal solar wind, and what does that tell us?
questions.do: Find the Carrington 1859 row in the How far to trust it table. Compare it with the Fastest measured button value.
questions.a: About 3,580 km/s, faster than any cloud ever measured (3,200 km/s). So the path was probably cleared by an earlier cloud that went first.
